title: Do the Gifts of the Spirit Still Happen?
excerpt: Tongues, prophecy and healing divide churches that confess the same Holy Spirit. Paul wrote three chapters to a church that had every gift and was misusing them, and those chapters still question the loud church and the quiet one alike.
body:
A woman grew up in a church where everyone prayed in tongues, and she never did. She was told to want it more, and by sixteen she had learned to move her lips. A man's church gathered around his wife's hospital bed and prayed for her healing with great confidence. She died in the spring, and a few weeks later someone he respected suggested, kindly, that there may have been doubt in the room. A college student from a quiet congregation visits a friend's church, where people raise their hands and a stranger says he has a word from the Lord for her, and she drives home unsure whether she has just seen a fraud or whether her own church has been missing something for two hundred years.

The skeptic has a clean way of putting it. The New Testament describes ordinary Christians healing the sick, prophesying and speaking languages they never learned. Either those things still happen, in which case the man on television selling miracle water speaks for God, or they do not, in which case it is fair to ask whether they ever did.

Before the argument, one thing has to be said to the man whose wife died. Christians read the Bible's promises about healing in more than one way, and this site's page for people facing a terminal diagnosis says of all of them: "None of these readings sets prayer against medical care, and none makes an unhealed believer guilty of too little faith. Paul prayed three times and was not healed, and no one in Scripture blames him." Nothing in this essay takes that back. If grief or illness has become too heavy to carry alone, [Find Help](/help) lists places to turn.

## What Paul Described

Almost everything the New Testament says about these gifts in detail is in three chapters of one letter, and Paul wrote them because a church was misusing what it had.

He begins with where the gifts come from and what they are for. "To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good" (1 Corinthians 12:7). He lists them without ranking the spectacular above the plain: wisdom, knowledge, faith, "gifts of healing," "the working of miracles," "prophecy," "various kinds of tongues" and their interpretation, all given by a Spirit "who apportions to each one individually as he wills" (1 Corinthians 12:9–11). No gift is given to everyone. "Do all possess gifts of healing? Do all speak with tongues?" (1 Corinthians 12:30). The Greek expects the answer no.

Then, between the chapter on gifts and the chapter on how to use them, he puts the chapter people read at weddings. "If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal" (1 Corinthians 13:1). It contains the sentence on which much of this debate turns: "As for prophecies, they will pass away; as for tongues, they will cease; as for knowledge, it will pass away. For we know in part and we prophesy in part, but when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away" (1 Corinthians 13:8–10).

The third chapter is practical, and it cuts in two directions. Paul wants the gifts: "earnestly desire the spiritual gifts, especially that you may prophesy" (1 Corinthians 14:1). He says, "I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you. Nevertheless, in church I would rather speak five words with my mind in order to instruct others, than ten thousand words in a tongue" (1 Corinthians 14:18–19). He limits speakers to two or three, one at a time, with an interpreter or not at all, and says that when prophets speak the others are to "weigh what is said" (1 Corinthians 14:29). His last word holds both halves together: "earnestly desire to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues. But all things should be done decently and in order" (1 Corinthians 14:39–40).

Two other texts set the frame. At Pentecost the disciples "began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance," and a crowd from many nations was bewildered "because each one was hearing them speak in his own language" (Acts 2:4, 6). Peter explained it from the prophet Joel: "in the last days it shall be, God declares, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy" (Acts 2:17). And the letter to the Hebrews, looking back, says the message of salvation "was attested to us by those who heard, while God also bore witness by signs and wonders and various miracles and by gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to his will" (Hebrews 2:3–4).

## What Happened Next

The gifts did not vanish when the last apostle died. Irenaeus, a bishop in Gaul late in the second century, wrote as a witness: "we do also hear many brethren in the Church, who possess prophetic gifts, and who through the Spirit speak all kinds of languages." Elsewhere he says that some Christians of his day drive out demons, some "see visions, and utter prophetic expressions," and "Others still, heal the sick by laying their hands upon them, and they are made whole."

In the same decades a movement in Asia Minor announced what it called the New Prophecy. Its leader, Montanus, and two women who prophesied with him claimed that the Spirit promised by Jesus now spoke through them. The wider church rejected the claim, and the experience left it wary of anyone who said, "The Spirit told me."

Two centuries later two of the most famous preachers of the age spoke of tongues as something they knew only from books. John Chrysostom, preaching through 1 Corinthians at Antioch, admitted that "This whole place is very obscure," and gave the reason: "our ignorance of the facts referred to and by their cessation, being such as then used to occur but now no longer take place." Augustine told his congregation that the tongues of Pentecost "were signs adapted to the time," given to show that the gospel would go to every language, and that the sign "passed away." Yet the same Augustine, near the end of his life, wrote that "even now miracles are wrought in the name of Christ," and he says they are little known even in the towns where they happen.

So the ancient record does not hand the argument to anyone. Prophecy and tongues are reported by a careful bishop around 180. By about 400 two of the church's best teachers treat tongues as past. Reports of healing never stop.

The Reformers inherited that settled view and had their own reasons to hold it. Rome pointed to the miracles of its saints as proof of its teaching, and some radicals claimed revelations that set Scripture aside. The Protestant answer was that God's word in Scripture is complete. The Westminster Confession of 1646 says that God committed his revelation "wholly unto writing," "those former ways of God's revealing his will unto his people being now ceased." In 1918 the Princeton theologian B. B. Warfield gave the position its classic modern form. He argued that miracles were the credentials of the apostles and died out with the generation they had laid hands on.

By then something else had begun. In April of 1906, in a former stable on Azusa Street in Los Angeles, a revival broke out under William Seymour, a preacher blind in one eye and the son of freed slaves. This site's history course tells it plainly: the city's newspapers mocked the meetings, and Black, white and immigrant believers worshiped together there in the decade of Jim Crow. From that room Pentecostalism spread until, a century later, the wider Pentecostal and charismatic family numbered somewhere over half a billion people by common estimates. From the 1960s on, the same experiences appeared inside the older churches, Catholic and Protestant. Whatever a Christian makes of this, it is now the faith of a large part of the world's church, and it began among people the culture counted last.

## Three Positions, Each in Its Own Terms

The cessationist is often heard as saying that God stopped doing miracles. He says nothing of the kind. He believes that God answers prayer and heals when he chooses. His claim is narrower. Certain gifts, apostleship, prophecy, tongues and the power to heal as a standing endowment of particular people, had a particular job, which was to lay the church's foundation and to mark the apostles' message as God's own. Paul says the church is "built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets" (Ephesians 2:20), and a foundation is laid once. Hebrews speaks of the signs in the past tense, as something that confirmed the message to an earlier generation. God, who spoke in many ways, "in these last days" has "spoken to us by his Son" (Hebrews 1:2), and that word is now written down and complete. What the cessationist fears is a second voice. Once "God told me" is allowed to stand beside the Bible, he believes, it will not be long before it stands above it.

The continuationist answers that the New Testament never says these gifts will stop before Christ returns. Paul ties their end to the day when we see "face to face" (1 Corinthians 13:12), and that day has not come. Peter said that the Spirit's outpouring belongs to "the last days," which in the New Testament means the whole time between Christ's two comings. Paul's commands still stand in every Bible: "Do not quench the Spirit. Do not despise prophecies, but test everything; hold fast what is good" (1 Thessalonians 5:19–21). Many continuationists add that prophecy in the churches was never Scripture's equal. It was to be weighed, which means it could be wrong, and so it threatens the Bible no more than a sermon does. What the continuationist fears is a church that confesses the Holy Spirit in its creed and expects nothing from him on a Sunday.

The Pentecostal goes a step further. He reads the book of Acts as a pattern for every generation and not only as a record of the first. In Acts believers receive the Spirit's power in an experience they can point to, and more than once they speak in tongues when it happens. Classical Pentecostal churches therefore teach a baptism in the Holy Spirit distinct from conversion, given for bold witness, with tongues as its first outward sign. Charismatic Christians in the older churches usually share the expectation without insisting on that sign. What the Pentecostal says to the rest of the church is simple. You believe the book of Acts happened, and you have arranged your churches so that it could never happen again.

Each has a question he finds hard. The cessationist is asked where the Bible says what he says, since his best verse about tongues ceasing is in a sentence that looks ahead to Christ's return. The continuationist is asked why two of the ancient church's greatest preachers thought tongues were gone, and how a prophecy that may be mistaken is a word from God. The Pentecostal is asked what to do with Paul's own question, "Do all speak with tongues?", and whether a second experience divides the church into two classes. A fourth group stands between them. It holds that Scripture rules out no gift today, and it tests every claim with care.

## Where It Has Gone Wrong

Abuses have followed this movement, and many Pentecostal and charismatic pastors are the first to name them. We have told the sick that they were not healed because they did not believe enough. Paul, who healed others, pleaded three times to be rid of his own affliction and was told, "My grace is sufficient for you" (2 Corinthians 12:9). He told Timothy to take a little wine for his "frequent ailments" (1 Timothy 5:23). He wrote, "I left Trophimus, who was ill, at Miletus" (2 Timothy 4:20). Whatever the gift of healing was in the apostles' hands, it was never a guarantee, and it was never a measure of the sick person's faith.

Prophecy has been used to control people. "The Lord told me" has ended arguments, arranged marriages and emptied bank accounts. And out of the healing revivals of the last century, joined, as this site's history course tells it, to the American creed of upward mobility, came the prosperity teaching, which reads God's favor in health and wealth and teaches the poor to give money in order to get it. [An earlier essay](/writing/can-a-christian-be-rich) says why that teaching is an error. It has done its worst harm among the sick and the poor, the people Azusa Street was for.

The opposite failure gets less attention, because it is quiet. There are churches that hold a careful doctrine of the Holy Spirit and expect nothing from God. We pray for the sick as a courtesy and would be alarmed if anyone recovered. James told the sick to "call for the elders of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord" (James 5:14), and many of us who honor the Bible have never once seen it done. We have taken Paul's rule about order and forgotten that he gave it to a church where things were happening. A doctrine that the sign gifts have ceased is one thing. A habit of mind in which God is thanked for the past and not asked for anything now is unbelief, whatever it calls itself, and no confession teaches it.

## What Paul Put in the Middle

The church at Corinth had every gift. Paul says so in his first lines: they were "not lacking in any gift" (1 Corinthians 1:7). The same church was split into parties, was taking its members to court and was getting drunk at the Lord's table. The gifts were real, and they proved nothing about the people who had them.

That is why the chapter on love stands where it does. Paul does not offer love as a better gift. He makes it the test of all of them. A tongue without love is noise. Prophecy and knowledge without it are, in his word, "nothing" (1 Corinthians 13:2). And he gives every church, loud or quiet, the same instruction to judge what it hears. "Test everything." John says the same: "do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God" (1 John 4:1). The first test Paul names is whether a voice confesses that "Jesus is Lord" (1 Corinthians 12:3). The second is whether the church is built up. A healing line that leaves the unhealed ashamed fails that test. So does a service so well guarded that no one could be surprised in it.

## What Is Settled and What Is Not

Christians confess together that the Holy Spirit is God, the Lord and giver of life, and that he is given to every believer: "Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him" (Romans 8:9). They confess that God hears prayer and is able to heal, and that Scripture is his authoritative word, with no voice today beside it or above it. Every position in this essay holds all of that.

Whether prophecy, tongues and gifts of healing continue as Paul described them, and whether there is a baptism in the Spirit after conversion, are questions of the second order. Faithful churches answer them differently, as this site's note on [1 Corinthians 12](/study/bible/1-corinthians/12) sets out, and this essay does not choose among them.

Whether a particular healing, word or experience was the work of God is a judgment for those who were there to weigh, and Paul told them to weigh it.

The skeptic's choice between the television healer and a closed heaven was never the only one, and the letter to Corinth is the proof. Paul believed the gifts were real, used them, and spent three chapters restraining them. But his letter leaves each kind of church with a question it would prefer not to be asked. The quiet church has to say what, exactly, it expects God to do. The loud church has to say whether it wants God or the experience of him. Paul's own answer to both is a sentence about what will be left when every gift is finished. "Now I know in part," he wrote (1 Corinthians 13:12), and he wrote it about himself.

*"Do not quench the Spirit. Do not despise prophecies, but test everything; hold fast what is good."* (1 Thessalonians 5:19–21)

*"Love never ends. As for prophecies, they will pass away; as for tongues, they will cease; as for knowledge, it will pass away."* (1 Corinthians 13:8)
